story.headline: The dollar rose a sixth straight day to its highest since April 2025, though Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gave no rate hint. Oil fell nearly 4% on surplus forecasts, and gold hit a 13-month low.

reads.policy: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh gave no hint on rates, so his colleagues' calls for a December hike still set the tone and bets stayed near certain. Canada's calm inflation figures cut the odds of a Bank of Canada hike to below even. Europe, Britain and Japan are still expected to hike, but US rates are rising faster, which keeps favouring the dollar.
reads.growth: A New York factory survey cooled sharply, though hiring in it was the strongest in four years, so it did little to the US picture. Euro-area factories barely grew, and Japan and China also came in soft. The US still looks firmer than most, and US retail sales on Tuesday are the next check.
reads.inflation: Canadian inflation held steady, with core prices near the Bank of Canada's goal, so energy costs are not yet spreading into everyday prices there. US inflation is still well above the Fed's goal, which keeps the pressure to hike. Falling oil should ease price worries a little, and UK inflation on Wednesday matters most for the pound.
reads.risk: US tech stocks fell sharply ahead of Nvidia's results, souring the mood. The Aussie and kiwi, which track market mood, slipped toward their lows. Yet the safe-haven franc and yen got little lift, because rising US rates still matter more to them than the scare.
reads.tot: Oil fell hard as traders bet that supply will outrun demand, with Gulf flows nearly back to normal. That helps energy buyers such as Japan and the euro area and takes support away from the Canadian dollar. Gold's slide to a 13-month low adds to the Aussie's troubles.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and the dollar's run keeps paying them. Their large bet on the yen keeps losing money as it weakens. Big bets against the euro, Aussie and kiwi could unwind fast on good news.
reads.fiscal: Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs above 5%. Higher yields support the dollar for now, but a growing deficit is a worry if buyers start asking for more. France's debt troubles keep weighing on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot inflation and firm talk from officials have made a December hike all but certain and lifted the dollar to its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, a half-point move a small minority bet; more hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal, and several officials say rates must rise again. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first speech since October was about AI and gave no reason to doubt them.
fed.watch: US retail sales Tuesday at 7:30 AM CT and minutes of the October meeting Wednesday at 1:00 PM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely; hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Canada's November jobs figures on December 4 and the path of oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi sits near a 19-month low.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting.
rbnz.watch: New Zealand inflation expectations tonight at 8:00 PM CT and Governor Anna Breman's speech Wednesday. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Economists see it as the last for now, which leaves the euro trailing as US rates keep rising.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, but factories are barely growing and France's debt worries linger, so the bank has little room to keep hiking.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Board member Hajime Takata called for an early move even though Japan's economy shrank slightly in the summer.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing import costs and prices up, and Takata says hikes are needed so it does not weaken further. A shrinking economy is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Whether Japan buys yen if the dollar tops 160 again, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech on November 30. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks, but hinted it may now pause. Weak Chinese figures, falling gold and a rising dollar have pushed the Aussie to its lowest since January.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is above the bank's forecasts, but unemployment is at a five-year high and demand from China, Australia's biggest customer, is softening.
rba.watch: Governor Michele Bullock speaks today at 4:50 PM CT, the November meeting minutes come Tuesday at 6:30 PM CT and jobs figures Wednesday at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. Markets still expect a second hike in December, though the pound has fallen six days in a row as US rates rise faster.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High energy costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation up, and chief economist Huw Pill says more rises are needed.
boe.watch: UK wage figures Tuesday at 1:00 AM CT and October inflation Wednesday at 1:00 AM CT, then Governor Andrew Bailey speaks twice. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by Democratic control of Congress. A sixth straight rise has taken it to its highest since April 2025 as December Fed hike bets hold near certain.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike is all but certain, and officials keep talking about more rises next year.
notes.inflation: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to raise rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. Rising US rates have pushed it to about $1.10, its lowest since April 2025.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected and may be the last for a while, while US rates keep rising, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Euro-area factories barely grew in September, business surveys have weakened and France's economy is struggling.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money from the region, though the latest fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. Faster-rising US rates have still pushed it lower six days in a row ahead of UK inflation figures on Wednesday.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK growth matched forecasts in the third quarter and business surveys are the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. A likely December rate hike and warnings from Japan's finance minister only just keep the dollar below 160 yen.

notes.policy: The Bank of Japan's rate is far below others, and even the December hike its board members are calling for leaves a wide gap with US rates.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did in early November, and loses some of that pull when they calm.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dear oil weighs on the yen, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, and those bets lose money as the yen weakens, which could make them close fast.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, but even a sharp fall in tech stocks has brought it little of that support lately.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks. It still fell to its lowest since January as US rates rose, China's economy slowed and gold slid.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause and some economists see the hikes ending.
notes.growth: Australian unemployment is at a five-year high, and weaker spending and factory output in China, its biggest customer, add to the drag.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells energy and metals abroad, but gold's slide to a 13-month low takes some of that support away.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but job losses and calm core inflation have cut bets on more hikes. Falling oil has pushed it near its weakest since spring.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, but calm core inflation has made a December move less likely than not.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Headline inflation holds above 3% on energy costs, and rising producer costs point to more pressure ahead, even though core prices sit near the bank's goal.
notes.tot: Oil still sits above pre-war levels, which gives the loonie a cushion, but forecasts of a supply surplus are pulling prices down fast.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. Rising US rates and weaker Chinese demand have kept it close to its lowest in 19 months.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, support its earnings, though China's spending is slowing.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
